newsitem.title: ITALY: ALPINE SKIING-SKIERS RUNNING ON TIGHT SCHEDULE.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-SKIERS RUNNING ON TIGHT SCHEDULE.

text.p: No-one is happy with the schedule for the Alpine world skiing championships, not even the International Ski Federation (FIS) who made it.
Having shoe-horned two weeks at Sestriere into a season already crowded with World Cup races, organisers and officials admit they have left little margin for disruption in the event of bad weather.

The busy schedule meant the women were competing in a World Cup race in Laax, Switzerland, on the day of the opening ceremony in Sestriere and they will ski their world championship downhill on a final day which also features the men's slalom.

"I personally believe we should have a different schedule," said FIS general secretary Gian Franco Kasper. "We should have designed it so there were some breaks before and after the world championships.

"But if you ask the the national ski associations and the race organisers they will say it's fine. The athletes themselves, if they have a free day they will go to an invitational race, they never complain about the number of races."

But Frenchman Luc Alphand, one of the favourites in the men's downhill, criticised the scheduling of the men's world championship super-G on Monday, only five days after they raced in the World Cup in Laax.
"There is no time for preparation, all you can do is rest and hope," complained Alphand.
French head coach Michele Vion said: "Serious problems will occur if we have even a little bad weather.
"Having the men's slalom on the last day is no problem but having the women's downhill on the same day is a big gamble. The problem is it's the women who always end up paying the bill."
In the event of bad weather it will be the women's downhill which will be sacrificed.
With the men's and women's speed events being run over the same course, the men's races were given priority, pushing the women's downhill and super-G into the second week.
While the championships are scheduled to end on Saturday February 15, organisers have left Sunday open just in case bad weather forces the women's downhill or training to be postponed.
But that would create a logistical nightmare for officials who would have to arrange extended stays in apartments and hotels for teams, volunteers and media.
The women would also be forced to re-arrange travel plans as they head directly to Japan after the championships for two World Cup downhills.
"The schedule here was difficult to make," said Kasper. "Actually the problems all started in Lillehammer when the girls wanted to ski on the men's courses.
"We did it at the Olympics and we did it again in Sierra Nevada but it just didn't work there.
"Sestriere had planned to build two downhill courses but when we changed in Lillehammer they of course didn't spend a lot of money building a second one.
"After Sierra Nevada we asked them to build a second course but it was too late.

"For that reason we had to reschedule the championships here in order to avoid overlapping and had to take the risk of putting the ladies' speed events at the end which without a doubt is a risk if we get bad weather."
